Thermal spraying can deposit coatings from a wide variety of feedstock materials, including metals, ceramics, and polymers.
Atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) can produce coatings with flame temperatures over 8000 K and particle velocities up to 500 m/s.

Suspension plasma spraying (SPS) and solution precursor plasma spraying (SPPS) enable the use of nano-sized feedstock particles, leading to coatings with different microstructures compared to traditional APS.
Low pressure plasma spraying (LPPS) and vacuum plasma spraying (VPS) can produce coatings with porosity as low as 1% and a columnar structure similar to physical vapor deposition.
Wire arc spraying is a cost-efficient thermal spray method, but the produced coatings have higher porosity and lower bond strength compared to other techniques.
Detonation gun (D-gun) spraying can reach flame temperatures around 4000 K and particle velocities up to 1000 m/s, resulting in coatings with better adhesion and lower porosity.
High velocity oxy-fuel (HVOF) spraying uses a supersonic gas jet to accelerate particles up to 1000 m/s, producing coatings with low porosity and high adhesion strength.
Cold spray (kinetic spraying) deposits particles without melting them, leading to coatings with low porosity, compressive residual stresses, and reduced in-flight oxidation.
Anti-microbial coatings can be designed to prevent bacterial adhesion, release anti-bacterial agents, or use immobilized biocidal compounds.
Anti-adhesive anti-microbial surfaces can help prevent antibiotic resistance but may lose functionality with wear, while coatings with embedded agents provide more targeted and continuous protection.
Thermal sprayed coatings have been used in a wide range of applications, including aerospace, electricity production, biomedical implants, and electronics.
